Baby & Child

Heart failure in babies and children: symptoms, causes and care

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Heart failure means that the heart and circulation are not meeting the body’s needs effectively. It does not mean the heart has stopped. In children, an abnormal route of blood flow, an obstruction, a heart-muscle problem or an abnormal rhythm can be responsible. A baby who tires during feeds and an older child who cannot manage usual activity may need different investigations and treatment.

What does congestive heart failure mean?

The heart normally sends blood to the lungs to receive oxygen and then to the body. Heart failure can develop even when the muscle squeezes reasonably well, if a structural problem makes circulation inefficient. It can also occur when the heart cannot pump or fill effectively. The diagnosis describes a clinical problem, not one specific defect.

Congestion means blood and fluid build up where they should not. Problems affecting the left heart can contribute to fluid in the lungs; right-sided problems can cause congestion in the liver and body’s veins. Both sides may be involved. This is different from cardiac arrest, although severe deterioration can be life-threatening.

Too much blood going to the lungs

Some congenital connections allow oxygen-rich blood to circulate back toward the lungs. Examples include a large ventricular septal defect, an opening between the two lower pumping chambers, and a patent ductus arteriosus, a fetal vessel between the pulmonary artery and aorta that remains open. A large duct can be important in a premature baby. The effect depends on the actual blood flow, not simply the presence of a hole.

An aortopulmonary window is an abnormal connection between the great arteries; truncus arteriosus involves a common arterial outlet. They are different defects that can also produce excessive lung blood flow. An isolated atrial septal defect, between the upper chambers, rarely causes heart failure in infancy. The cardiologist explains which anatomy matters for that child.

Obstruction, heart-muscle disease and rhythm problems

Critical aortic-valve narrowing, coarctation of the aorta or an underdeveloped left heart can obstruct effective blood flow to the body. These are not all the same as a primarily weak heart muscle. Some newborns become seriously ill as fetal connections close, so an apparently comfortable first day does not guarantee safety.

Cardiomyopathy affects the heart muscle; myocarditis is inflammation of it. Infections, inherited or other diseases and persistent abnormal rhythms can contribute. Kawasaki disease can affect the heart and coronary arteries. A rhythm that is too fast or too slow may impair pumping. Babies as well as older children can have myocardial or rhythm-related failure, sometimes without an obvious structural defect.

Signs in babies: feeding, breathing and growth

A baby may tire, sweat or stop early during milk feeds, take less milk or gain weight slowly. Rapid or laboured breathing and a fast heartbeat can increase the effort of feeding. Some babies have less energy or become unusually sleepy; swelling around the eyes, feet or abdomen can occur. A forceful visible heartbeat or a small appearance alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

A clinician assesses growth over time, breathing, circulation and signs such as an enlarged liver or unusual heart sounds. Some children need developmental support too. New or worsening feeding fatigue, sweating, reduced intake, swelling or poor growth needs urgent same-day advice from the child’s team. Breathing difficulty, abnormal colour or reduced responsiveness needs emergency help instead.

Why symptoms do not always start at birth

After birth, blood flow changes as resistance in the lungs falls. A baby with a large left-to-right shunt may initially feed well and develop increasing breathing or feeding difficulty over the following weeks. The timing varies; there is no guaranteed symptom-free first fortnight or fixed week when failure must appear.

A severe obstruction or myocardial problem may cause illness much earlier, including in the first days. A normal earlier examination, apparently normal pulses or no obvious murmur cannot exclude later deterioration. Do not wait for a scheduled check or a particular age if the baby becomes unwell.

How it may appear in an older child

An older child may become breathless or unusually tired with walking, stairs or play they previously managed. Appetite may fall, weight gain may slow or weight may be lost. Conversely, fluid retention can cause swelling and rapid weight gain. Cough, abdominal discomfort or a swollen liver may be part of the picture; a clinician may hear a gallop rhythm.

Chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness also need attention. Compare the child’s abilities with their usual pattern rather than assuming every difference from a friend means disease. Fainting during exercise is an emergency, even if the child then seems better. Stop activity and obtain help; do not test whether the symptoms recur.

Which changes need immediate help?

Call emergency services for very fast or difficult breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale or blotchy colour, cold or clammy/damp skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, a floppy or hard-to-wake child, a seizure or a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry. In babies under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment; a temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours in a baby or young child also needs immediate emergency assessment. A child does not need every sign.

Chest pain, a new fast or irregular heartbeat, new confusion, drowsiness or dizziness in a child with suspected or known heart disease also warrants immediate emergency help. Fainting during exercise must not wait for a routine appointment. Do not drive the unwell child yourself: arrange another driver or an ambulance as advised. For other new feeding, growth, swelling or exercise concerns, seek urgent same-day clinical advice rather than relying on an app or home monitor.

How the team investigates heart failure

Assessment starts with the history, feeding and growth pattern, examination and vital signs. Echocardiography shows structure, blood flow and muscle function; an ECG records electrical activity and rhythm. Chest imaging can show heart size and lung congestion. Blood tests may check organ function, body salts and other clues. These findings are interpreted together, not as a home checklist.

Some children need cardiac MRI, catheterization to measure pressures or clarify anatomy, selected genetic or infection investigations, or a supervised exercise test when appropriate and stable. Not every child needs every test. The team should explain the suspected cause and the immediate plan; tests must not delay stabilization of an acutely unwell child.

Medicines must fit the cause and the child

A diuretic such as furosemide helps remove excess fluid through the kidneys. Other selected medicines, including ACE inhibitors or beta blockers, may reduce workload or help particular types of myocardial dysfunction. Digoxin can be useful in selected pumping or rhythm problems. These are examples, not a universal first-line combination: drugs used for muscle failure are not automatically appropriate for every left-to-right shunt.

The cardiology team selects the medicine, formulation and dose and monitors effects such as blood pressure, heart rate, kidney function and electrolytes. Check before adding nonprescription or herbal products, and ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose. Do not change doses, stop treatment, double a dose or impose salt or fluid restrictions yourself. A new concerning symptom needs advice rather than assuming it is only a medicine effect.

Repairing a defect or treating a rhythm

Medicines may control symptoms while a child is assessed for repair; they do not close a structural defect. Some ventricular openings become smaller or close naturally, but waiting for growth is not appropriate for every large symptomatic defect. An aortopulmonary window, truncus arteriosus, critical obstruction or complex left-heart condition may need early intervention, sometimes in stages. Timing follows anatomy and the child’s condition.

A slow rhythm may require a pacemaker; some fast rhythms need medicines or a catheter procedure such as ablation. Repair, palliation and rhythm treatment have different goals and risks. Some children recover good function; others need ongoing treatment or further procedures. Ask what the proposed intervention can achieve and what it cannot promise.

Nutrition is part of treatment

Extra work of breathing and feeding can use energy needed for growth. A dietitian and feeding team may prescribe fortified breast milk, higher-calorie formula or a different feeding schedule. Breastfeeding support can remain valuable. A nasogastric tube carries milk from the nose into the stomach and can reduce feeding effort while delivering the nutrition the child needs; it is not intended to deprive the child of calories.

Selected older children also need nutritional or tube-feeding support. The route, amount and any fluid limit are individualized. Do not concentrate or dilute milk, force feeds or give extra water without the team’s instructions. Ask for a written preparation and feeding plan and what to do if intake falls, vomiting occurs or medicines cannot be kept down.

Hospital care and advanced support

A child who deteriorates may need hospital medicines and breathing or circulatory support. Oxygen is prescribed according to the anatomy and clinical situation: changing lung and body blood flow can matter in some congenital defects. This is not a reason to withhold emergency care or adjust prescribed oxygen at home. Use the cardiac team’s specific targets and response plan.

For selected advanced failure, ECMO or a ventricular assist device can support circulation during recovery or while awaiting transplant. Some devices offer longer-term support; a total artificial heart is an option only for selected patients, not every baby or everyone unsuitable for transplant. Body size, anatomy, risks, available expertise and family goals guide decisions. Transplant is one possible pathway, with its own lifelong treatment and follow-up.

Activity, outlook and a workable family plan

The outlook depends on the cause, severity, response and any remaining disease. Treating a reversible problem or repairing a defect can improve function, but neither a normal life nor progressive decline can be predicted for every child. Cardiomyopathy may improve in some circumstances or progress in others. Keep cardiology follow-up even when symptoms improve, and discuss growth, development, school needs and emotional support.

Agree an activity plan with the cardiac team. Some children need limits or supervised rehabilitation; others can enjoy a range of activities. Swimming is not automatically safe for every child with heart failure, and a blanket ban on all play is not an individualized plan. Keep medicine and feeding instructions, contact details and warning thresholds available to caregivers. New symptoms and emergency signs take priority over recording data or waiting for the next visit.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the cardiology team which mechanism is causing failure, what tests are needed and whether medicines are controlling symptoms or an intervention is needed. Do not use a defect’s name alone to predict the plan.

Keep written medicine, milk-preparation, feeding and any fluid or oxygen instructions. Check doses and formulations with the team, and ask how to respond to vomiting, reduced intake or a missed dose.

Agree follow-up, school and activity arrangements and an emergency response plan with all caregivers. Seek help for new symptoms rather than waiting for a log, monitor reading or routine appointment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize feeding and growth observations, prescribed medicines, appointment questions and the team’s care plan. It cannot diagnose heart failure, interpret an echocardiogram, set oxygen or fluid targets, choose milk concentration or judge whether a child is stable. Tracking must not delay medical help.

When to seek help

Seek immediate emergency help for difficult or very fast breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, floppiness, difficulty waking, a seizure or a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment. A temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours in a baby or young child also needs immediate emergency assessment. Chest pain, new rhythm problems, confusion, drowsiness or dizziness in suspected heart disease, and fainting during exercise, are emergency warnings too. Do not drive the unwell child yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance as advised. Seek urgent same-day advice for other new feeding, growth, swelling or exercise changes. Do not alter cardiac medicines, oxygen, fluid or milk preparation without the treating team.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Heart failure describes ineffective circulation, not a heart that has stopped; several different childhood mechanisms can cause it.
  • Feeding fatigue, sweating and poor growth in babies, or declining activity in older children, need clinical assessment.
  • Breathing, colour or responsiveness changes and fainting during exercise can require immediate emergency help.
  • Medicines, repair, feeding support and advanced devices are selected for the actual cause; do not alter treatment or milk preparation yourself.
  • Follow-up, activity and outlook are individual, with support for the child and family beyond the next procedure.

Frequently asked questions

How is heart failure treated in a baby or child?

Treatment follows the cause and severity. It may include selected medicines, nutritional support, repair of a defect or rhythm treatment. Some children need hospital or advanced device/transplant care. Medicines may control symptoms without repairing the anatomy; no single regimen or operation suits everyone.

Can a well-squeezing heart still be involved?

Yes. An abnormal connection can send excessive blood back to the lungs even when the muscle squeezes well. Obstruction, myocardial disease and rhythm problems are other mechanisms. The team determines which applies rather than diagnosing from the word failure alone.

What signs can appear in a baby?

Tiring or sweating during feeds, reduced intake, slow growth, fast breathing, less energy or swelling can occur. These signs have other causes too. New feeding or growth changes need urgent advice; difficult breathing, abnormal colour, floppiness or difficulty waking needs emergency help.

Can a child lead an active life?

Many children improve with treatment, but the outlook depends on the actual condition and response. Some need lifelong medicines, procedures or activity adjustments. Ask for individualized advice about play, school and sport; neither guaranteed recovery nor inevitable decline is accurate for every child.

Can symptoms begin after a reassuring newborn check?

Yes. Circulation changes after birth, and some shunts cause increasing symptoms over weeks. Severe obstruction or muscle disease may present earlier. A normal previous check is not a reason to ignore new breathing, feeding or responsiveness changes.

Does every child need all the heart tests?

No. History, examination, echo and ECG often guide care; blood tests, imaging, catheterization, genetics or supervised exercise testing are selected for the findings. A child who is acutely unwell needs stabilization rather than waiting for a complete outpatient test list.

Should I add more formula powder or water to help?

Do not change milk concentration or fluid intake yourself. The feeding and cardiac teams may prescribe extra calories or tube feeding, but the exact preparation, volume and schedule must fit the child. Ask for written instructions and prompt advice if feeding worsens.

When should we get emergency help?

Get immediate help for difficult or very fast breathing, blue/grey or unusually pale/blotchy colour, cold or damp skin, fainting or loss of consciousness, floppiness, difficulty waking, seizure or a weak/high-pitched/continuous cry. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more needs immediate emergency assessment. A temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours in a baby or young child also needs immediate emergency assessment. Chest pain, new rhythm problems, confusion, drowsiness or dizziness with suspected heart disease, and fainting during exercise, are also emergency warnings. Do not drive the unwell child yourself or wait for all signs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
